title: Stochastic Finite-Transition Learning and Exploration for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
abstract: Generative MRI reconstruction maps an initial source distribution to the target image distribution along a learned recovery trajectory. Common generative methods, such as diffusion and flow, typically learn fine-grained local dynamics whose integration defines this global mapping, hence requiring many network evaluations at inference. Existing few-step sampling approaches can lower computational burden by approximating large transformations from local dynamics, albeit at the expense of reconstruction fidelity. FLEX-MRI instead partitions recovery into a small number of finite intervals between retained states defined by progressive changes in k-space support, and directly learns the reconstruction change across each interval. Because such finite transitions can admit multiple plausible outcomes, FLEX-MRI combines support-relaxed finite-transition learning with stochastic exploration. During training, randomized k-space sampling masks define finite-transition targets with varying support, while the prediction loss remains unrestricted by each individual mask. At inference, FLEX-MRI perturbs a random subset of currently estimated k-space coefficients, allowing the learned predictor to stochastically explore alternative transition paths. Each predicted state is then reconciled with the acquired measurements through data consistency. We theoretically show that this stochastic exploration induces nonzero transition-level variation through the learned recovery map and data consistency without requiring an auxiliary generative sampler. Experiments on multi-coil MRI datasets show that FLEX-MRI outperforms competing methods while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to few-step baselines.

title: CaptchaAgent: Verifiable Visual Reasoning for CAPTCHA Solving
abstract: Modern reasoning CAPTCHAs require fine-grained perception, compositional relation reasoning, and grounded browser interaction. End-to-end vision-language model agents remain brittle in this setting because a missed object, incorrect count, or confused relation can propagate directly to the final action. To address this problem, we present CaptchaAgent, a structured visual reasoning framework for interactive CAPTCHA solving. Instead of predicting an action directly from a screenshot, CaptchaAgent first constructs a visual intermediate representation (V-IR) that explicitly records entities, attributes, and spatial or topological relations. A symbol-only ASCII protocol further requires the parser to commit to a concrete object set and count. Building on this global representation, localized evidence refinement revisits ambiguous regions at higher effective resolution, while counterfactual consistency verification tests whether the resulting action remains stable under task-preserving transformations. Across three proprietary backbones on Open CaptchaWorld, CaptchaAgent improves Pass@1 by 21.3-25.8 percentage points over a commercially available browser agent baseline evaluated with the same backbones. On the separate offline Oedipus-data benchmark, it further improves average Pass@1 by 9.2-12.3 percentage points over the Oedipus solver across three matched backbones. The intermediate traces show that exact counting, continuous geometry, and ordered execution remain major sources of automation difficulty for the evaluated agents, providing practical guidance for designing more resilient compositional CAPTCHAs.

title: A pair-primary associative substrate with exact in-band episodic memory
abstract: We build a GPU-resident associative memory whose unit of representation is a relation: an ordered word pair with a signed binding strength, in place of the token. One rule drives all writes. On each exposure the binding state moves a fixed fraction of the way toward a ceiling that the world asserts. The rule admits an exact in-band episodic trace. Each binding carries six accumulators with distinct decay rates; together they form a sufficient statistic for the binding's exposure history. The ordered sequence of asserted targets follows by inverting the resulting generalized Vandermonde system. Count recovers exactly on all 4,640 live bindings (the complete live web, not a sample). Order recovers on the production bank to 1.5e-10 in float64 at depth six (2.4e-13 at depth three), and to 1.2e-3 through the production float32 kernels at four-step histories. The exactness claim is conditional: at least as many distinct, well-separated rates as history depth, and precision exceeding the conditioning (section 3.5). Those conditions collapse to one law, error ≈ ratio × cond(V) × precision (median ratio 0.03-0.05 over a six-order-of-magnitude sweep), so a unit's exactness envelope is computable before it is built (section 3.6). The rate set follows by minimizing cond(V), 867× better-conditioned than the reference (section 3.7). Pairing two rate bands lifts the exact depth from six to nine in float64, past the M ≥ k count wall (section 3.8). A shared-state control runs the identical law in a linear-attention layout. One binding alone on a shared state recovers exactly; at one thousand shared pairs the worst pair errs at 1.7e3 while the pair-primary arm holds at 1e-12 across all populations. The write-landing site, not the read geometry, carries the difference. Replaying the recorded input ledger rebuilds 9,272 of 9,296 nonzero live bindings, 99.7 percent. The two theorems supply state-only inversion for the organ-backed quantities, count and order.

title: Code and results for "Similarity-Metric Sensitivity in Hard and Soft Clustering" (v1.0)
abstract: Code, per-trial results, and figures for the article "Similarity-Metric Sensitivity in Hard and Soft Clustering: A Statistically Grounded Comparison of K-Means, Fuzzy C-Means, and K-Nearest Neighbors, with a Mineral-Composition Case Study" (A. V. Shinde, D. D. Patil, B. A. Ahire, S. S. Bhavsar; submitted to Results in Engineering, 2026). The Python pipeline compares K-Means, Fuzzy C-Means, and a supervised KNN reference under the Euclidean, Manhattan, Cosine, and Pearson metrics. Each metric uses a matched estimator (spherical k-means, correlation clustering, k-medians, fuzzy c-medians), and all metrics run on the same standardised features. It covers Iris, Wine, WDBC, and a de-circularised synthetic mineral-composition dataset, with 30 bootstrap-resampled trials per configuration. Included: the experiment and statistics scripts (two-way ANOVA, bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation tests, pooled variance partition, TOST equivalence tests), the per-trial results, the generated LaTeX tables, and all figures. All randomness is seeded and the stored results are reproduced exactly. See README.md for the run order.

title: Information Provenance and Conservative Enrichment in Prospective Health
abstract: Description Prospective Health evaluates present organizational realization together with the adequacy of lawful, constitutively viable continuations under declared conditions. This fourth paper in the Health, Formally Defined series establishes a machine-checked finite benchmark for examining how information enters, survives, and is transformed throughout that measurement architecture. A five-state forest system provides a complete formal setting in which contextual admissibility, constitutive continuation, response observation, capacity representation, and Health judgments can be examined exhaustively. Two equivalent history encodings establish invariance under relocating contextual restrictions between dependent history constructors and an explicit lawfulness predicate. The resulting candidate–lawful–viable response pipeline identifies the precise contribution of each semantic filter. The benchmark establishes an exact information-refinement ladder with five detailed-response classes, four original-capacity classes, and three classes distinguished by the complete declared Health language. Machine-checked classification results identify every distinction lost through representational compression and every additional distinction retained by capacity but unused by the established Health queries. A general conservative-capacity-refinement lemma gives sufficient conditions for preserving existing Health judgments under representational enrichment. A strict forest instance demonstrates how additional response information can support new queries while preserving established adequacy through exact projection. The results establish a formally verified reference for information provenance, observation sufficiency, and conservative evolution of Health representations. Their scope is the declared finite dynamics and set-valued capacity semantics. Extensions to probability-weighted capacity require compatible stochastic laws and preservation of query-relevant events. The companion empirical-synthetic measurement study investigates these additional obligations under incomplete ecological observations, uncertain dynamics, and numerical inference.

title: Reward-Quality Divergence (RQD): Code, Saved Runs and Analysis Scripts (Anonymous Review Artifact)
abstract: Anonymous review artifact for the paper Reward-Quality Divergence: Telling Judge Gaming from Judge Error in Visual RL. Please do not try to identify the authors. RQD measures the gap between a judge's reward and an anchor-based quality score during reinforcement learning, subtracts the gap that exists before training (the floor), and labels the remaining gap growth as gaming, drift, collapse or none. Contents Code: the measure, the anchor checker, the judge wrapper with its prompt, the control rewards, the second grader and the re-scoring job. Results: the saved answers, rewards and anchor scores of all 154 training runs reported in the paper, plus the re-scoring and second-grader results. Analysis scripts: CPU-only scripts that rebuild every table of the paper from the saved results in a few minutes. Data: item files with the question, reference answer and anchor fact of every item (no images; the images come from the public ChartQA, GQA and DocVQA datasets). Human labels: the 100 human correctness labels used to check the anchor. Checks included: one script recomputes the anchor score of all 219,500 saved answers from the item files and the released checker and compares it with the stored score; unit tests cover the measure, the anchor and the rewards. The GRPO training loop and the cluster job scripts are not part of this review artifact; they will be released with the published paper. All training settings are listed in the paper's appendix. Code: MIT license. Result files and human labels: CC BY 4.0. The datasets keep their original licenses. See README.md for the commands.

title: Physical-state supervision for design-only Gaussian process surrogates of implosion simulations: supporting data
abstract: Supporting research data for physical-state supervision of design-only Gaussian process surrogates, with optional mixture-of-experts comparisons. Includes 1,987 CH designs, 3,000 thermal-explosion designs, 3,000 recalculated Be/Cocktail designs, state diagnostics, saved predictions, paired evaluation metrics, learning curves, grid diagnostics, timing records and file-level provenance. The data record does not include software, solver binaries, material libraries or raw trajectories. Grid sensitivities and historical reproduction limitations are documented in README.md. Data and accompanying documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0.

title: Adaptive Group Feature Stream Selection for Dynamic Feature Stream
abstract: Feature selection is a dimensionality reduction technique that identifies relevant features while discarding irrelevant and redundant ones. Traditional feature selection methods require the entire feature space to be known in advance, making them suitable for static datasets. However, in real-world applications such as healthcare monitoring, sensor networks, and image analysis, new features are generated at different time intervals. In dynamic feature streams, the entire feature space is not known beforehand. To address this challenge, this paper proposes Adaptive Group Feature Stream Selection (AGFS), an online feature selection framework for dynamic feature streams. The proposed framework extends the Alpha-Investing algorithm from processing features individually to processing features that arrive in randomly sized groups. It employs a multi-stage processing approach. First, variance filtering removes constant features. Next, Alpha-Investing-based statistical testing selects relevant feature groups. A group-size capping mechanism is introduced to prevent larger feature groups from being discarded during statistical testing. Within each selected group, features are ranked using feature-class correlation, and redundant features are removed using correlation-based redundancy removal. A data-driven threshold, computed from feature-class correlation observed so far, is introduced to help prevent unnecessary elimination of complementary features. An adaptive wealth mechanism rewards the selection of informative features. Experiments conducted on six benchmark datasets using a K-Nearest Neighbours classifier with 5-fold cross-validation, demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves higher average classification accuracy (87.36%) while maintaining a competitive number of selected features compared to existing feature selection methods. The proposed approach is also validated across multiple classifiers and its consistency across classifiers is reported.

Within each selected group, features are ranked using feature-class correlation, and redundant features are removed using correlation-based redundancy removal. A data-driven threshold, computed from feature-class correlation observed so far, is introduced to help prevent unnecessary elimination of complementary features. An adaptive wealth mechanism rewards the selection of informative features. Experiments conducted on six benchmark datasets using a K-Nearest Neighbours classifier with 5-fold cross-validation, demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves higher average classification accuracy (87.36%) while maintaining a competitive number of selected features compared to existing feature selection methods. The proposed approach is also validated across multiple classifiers and its consistency across classifiers is reported.

title: AI and Corporate Strategy: HorizonAI
abstract: Business strategy has evolved dramatically over the past century. Applying new and improved organizational and strategic methodologies in tandem with AI reshapes strategy by providing actionable intelligence across the three domains of leadership. In this chapter, the authors begin with the horizon scanning/scenario planning component of strategic fitness, with organizational excellence and growth creation. In the past, scenario planning was restricted to strategy and R&D offices. HorizonAI is a structured framework blending human strategic foresight with AI's analytical muscle. It consists of four steps: Observe, Attack, Orient, and Adapt (OAOA). AI is revolutionizing scenario planning by transforming what was once a lengthy, periodic exercise into a continuous, data-driven process. To institutionalize adaptation, many firms now embed AI into executive decision meetings. AI is the enabler, not the replacement, for human strategic foresight.

title: TraceSampler: Making Sampling Errors Predictable and Correctable for Accelerated Generative Sampling
abstract: Accurate sampling from continuous-time generative models can require many model evaluations. Low-step sampling reduces cost, but coarse updates introduce endpoint errors that can accumulate and degrade generation quality. We introduce TraceSampler, a post-training method that corrects these errors without modifying the pretrained model. Rather than optimising low-step updates directly, TraceSampler models endpoint error as a sample-specific prediction problem. A higher-step reference integration over the same interval provides the supervised target, while a compact representation makes high-dimensional error predictable from the sampling trace. This representation combines shared residual structure, trace-derived directions, and a low-rank remainder, so shallow per-step MLP heads predict sample-dependent coefficients. These coefficients drive a two-stage learned residual correction: the first stage predicts the full endpoint residual, while an intermediate backbone evaluation provides new trace information to predict the remaining residual; this evaluation is reused by the following step. TraceSampler is evaluated with Rectified Flow on CIFAR-10, SiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, and SD3.5 Medium for text-to-image generation. At 10 steps, it reduces trajectory MSE relative to matched-step Euler by 90.5% on CIFAR-10 and 85.6% on ImageNet-256, while achieving FID scores of 2.692 and 2.189, close to 120-step Heun references of 2.601 and 2.056 with 24$\times$ fewer backbone evaluations. On SD3.5 Medium, TraceSampler improves image quality and prompt following; at 10 steps, ImageReward rises from 0.752 to 0.906 while trajectory MSE falls by 70.7%. These gains preserve Euler's backbone-evaluation budget, add less than 0.4% inference FLOPs, and incur negligible wall-clock overhead, showing that coarse-step sampling error can be made predictable from the sampling trace and efficiently corrected.

title: Host-Aware Web Crawling for LLM Pretraining Data
abstract: Web crawling is a major source of large language model (LLM) pretraining data, yet data-selection pipelines discard a large share of crawled pages. We investigate how a crawler should allocate its budget across and within hosts to collect more high-quality pretraining data. Combining document-level quality classifier scores, web-graph centrality metrics, and Common Crawl's per-host crawl coverage, we find that roughly half of the variation in classifier scores occurs between hosts. In the crawls we analyze, a few pages from a host also provide a useful estimate of the quality of its remaining pages. Common Crawl uses harmonic centrality, a graph centrality metric, to guide its crawl allocation. In our simulations, using centrality to choose which hosts to crawl yields limited gains over random ordering and performs worse for some classifiers. For deciding how deeply to crawl each host, sampling a few pages and then fetching more from hosts with higher-scoring samples collects several times more high-quality pages per fetch than uniform depth or centrality-based allocation. Finally, Common Crawl's observed per-host coverage has little correlation with the evaluated quality signals. We estimate that tens of millions of high-quality pages remain among known but uncrawled URLs in each crawl examined, with most concentrated on a small share of hosts.

title: Robust Langevin Sampling under State-Dependent Heavy-Tailed Noise with Applications to LLM Fine-Tuning
abstract: Existing convergence guarantees for non-log-concave sampling with stochastic gradient Langevin Monte Carlo (SG-LMC) typically assume globally Lipschitz gradients and uniformly bounded noise variance. Both assumptions can fail even in elementary sampling problems, and relaxing them better reflects practical applications such as Bayesian fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). We relax both assumptions through generalized smoothness and our proposed state-dependent heavy-tailed oracle with finite $p$-th moments, $1<p\leq 2$. The oracle permits infinite variance when $p<2$ and includes the Blum-Gladyshev (BG-0) condition. We study these relaxations separately and jointly, proposing three methods. Under globally Lipschitz gradients, robust LMC (R-LMC) handles the proposed oracle through geometric-median centering and residual clipping. With exact gradients, adaptive LMC (A-LMC) controls discretization error under generalized smoothness. Robust adaptive LMC (RA-LMC) addresses both relaxations through robust estimation and a noise-aware step size. For all three methods, we establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees in Fisher information (FI) without assuming dissipativity or a functional inequality. Synthetic experiments demonstrate FI convergence and the benefit of each mechanism. Bayesian fine-tuning experiments with LLMs and vision-language models support our oracle model and show that RA-LMC matches or outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

title: Guide pour une intégration réussie de l’IA au sein des organisations
abstract: Plusieurs organisations (publiques, privées et à but non lucratif) ont intégré des outils d’IA dans leurs activités ou sont en train de se familiariser avec ceux-ci. Cependant, de nombreuses études montrent que, malgré des attentes élevées et des investissements importants, la plupart d’entre elles n’ont pas encore constaté de gains mesurables en matière de productivité, de chiffre d’affaires ou de retour sur investissement. Le retour sur investissement peut tarder à se concrétiser, puisque les grandes innovations technologiques mettent souvent plus de dix ans à produire des retombées économiques mesurables. L’objectif de ce guide est de fournir aux organisations des stratégies pour intégrer avec succès les outils d’IA et de proposer de bonnes pratiques permettant d’utiliser ces outils de manière efficace et responsable. La version préliminaire du guide s’appuie sur une revue des lignes directrices, des cadres et des guides sur l’intégration de l’IA publiés par des organisations publiques, privées et à but non lucratif au Canada et à l’international, ainsi que sur des études scientifiques récentes. Le guide a ensuite été bonifié à partir des résultats de l'étude, qui repose sur des données recueillies auprès de gestionnaires, de développeurs et de formateurs de quatre secteurs au Québec : l’économie sociale et l’action communautaire, la finance, les ressources humaines et les technologies de l’information.

title: Convergence Between Artificial Intelligence and Digital Purchasing Behavior
authors: Célia Maria Ramos Serra Reis Barroso
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming digital behavior and consumer decision-making, reshaping interactions between individuals and brands across digital platforms. This chapter analyzes the relationship between digital behavior, AI, and marketing strategies in a changing technological context. It examines how AI-driven tools, such as predictive analytics and automated recommendation systems, enable content personalization, improve user experiences, and increase marketing effectiveness. Based on contemporary literature and secondary data from sources including Statista, Pew Research Center, Pordata and Euromonitor, the study adopts an exploratory approach to assess AI's impact on consumer engagement and strategic marketing practices. It also discusses ethical challenges, such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, and manipulation risks. The research offers insights for scholars and practitioners on AI's growing influence and highlights the need for future qualitative studies on consumer perceptions.

title: A Hybrid deep learning model for effective segmentation and classification of lung nodules from CT images
abstract: Deep learning algorithms will be used to detect lung nodule anomalies at an earlier stage. The primary goal of this effort is to properly identify lung cancer, which is critical in preserving a person’s life. Lung cancer has been a source of concern for people all around the world for decades. Several researchers presented numerous issues and solutions for various stages of a computer-aided system for diagnosing lung cancer in its early stages, as well as information about lung cancer. Computer vision is one of the field of artificial intelligence this is a better way to detect and prevent the lung cancer. This study focuses on the stages involved in detecting lung tumor regions, namely pre-processing, segmentation, and classification models. An adaptive median filter is used in pre-processing to identify the noise. The work’s originality seeks to create a simple yet effective model for the rapid identification and U-net architecture based segmentation of lung nodules. This approach focuses on the identification and segmentation of lung cancer by detecting picture normalcy and abnormalities.

title: Role-Guided Risk-Aware Attention for Multi-AUV Target-Zone Reaching under Active Defense
abstract: Cooperative target-zone reaching by multiple autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) under active defense remains challenging because each vehicle must make sequential guidance decisions under nonlinear hydrodynamics, sonar-limited perception, obstacle constraints, and defender interference. This paper proposes a role-guided risk-aware attention variant of multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG), termed role-guided risk-aware attention MADDPG (RGRA-MADDPG), for attacker-side multi-AUV target-zone reaching under active defense. Different from homogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) policies, the proposed method assigns mission-specific roles to the AUVs, including a Primary Attack AUV, a Coordinated Strike AUV, and a Bait AUV. A role-conditioned attention module is developed to help each AUV selectively emphasize targets, defenders, obstacles, and teammates from local observations, while a risk-prior bias introduces interpretable obstacle-, defender-, and target-related cues into the attention scores. The framework is trained under centralized training and executed through decentralized local policies. Comparative simulations, perturbation tests, mechanism-isolation studies, and physical-response validation are used to evaluate target-reaching success, cooperative behavior, robustness, and command feasibility. Results show that the proposed method improves adversarial target-zone reaching performance over standard MADDPG-based variants while producing differentiated and interpretable multi-AUV tactics.

title: Real-Time Traffic Density Estimation: A Hybrid Computer Vision and Predictive Machine Learning Pipeline
abstract: Traffic density estimation from camera feeds requires connecting visual perception with short-horizon forecasting. We present a two-stage pipeline that combines vehicle detection and tracking with a spatial logic layer, followed by a temporal estimator. The spatial layer filters bounding boxes by their overlap with a precomputed road mask and extracts per-frame traffic features. LSTM, GRU, and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) estimators use these features to predict five future steps from a ten-frame input window. We benchmark ten detector variants from six families on a dataset of 5,716 annotated frames using a single NVIDIA GPU. YOLOv5l achieves the highest mAP@50:95 of 0.524 at 56 frames per second, while YOLOv8n reaches 258 frames per second at 0.487 mAP@50:95; these rates measure detector inference without tracking or spatial filtering. Temporal evaluation on 29,243 held-out windows yields aggregate R-squared values of 0.858 for GRU, 0.856 for LSTM, and 0.840 for TCN. These metrics measure forecasts of detector-derived telemetry and are dominated by direction variance, rather than establishing absolute traffic-density accuracy. No road mask was available for the evaluation stream, limiting validation of the spatial filtering component. A live run on a third camera stream examines forecasting behavior within the complete pipeline. The results characterize detector speed-accuracy trade-offs and the limitations of short-window traffic telemetry forecasting.

title: SBNO : Schrödinger Bridge Neural Operator for the Forward and Inverse Problems under Missing Information
abstract: Partial differential equation (PDE) surrogate modeling often relies on either dense observations or access to governing equations/physics constraints. In practice, observations can be sparse and partial, and the underlying physics may be partially specified or unavailable. We introduce SBNO, an equation-free paired-data diffusion bridge matching framework that learns conditional operators for both forward and inverse PDE problems under partial observations. SBNO uses diffusion Schrödinger bridge matching to learn a pair of time-dependent drifts from a mask-aware endpoint coupling that preserves empirical input-solution pairing during training and supports both PDE-task directions within a single framework. At inference time, SBNO produces a deterministic point reconstruction by integrating the probability-flow ODE constructed from the learned drift pair, without inference-time observation or PDE guidance-weight tuning. On five PDE benchmarks with 5% observations, SBNO achieves superior or comparable accuracy to baselines while demonstrating lower test-instance error dispersion. Furthermore, SBNO is at least $9.7 \times$ faster and reduces GPU memory by at least $4.3 \times$ compared to guided-diffusion baselines.

title: A robust digital receiver architecture for continuous-variable quantum key distribution
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution utilizes advanced digital signal processing techniques to mitigate channel impairments, driving the progress of high-performance quantum secure communications. Specifically, digital heterodyne receivers are commonly implemented using down-conversion algorithms to detect both components simultaneously where the signal is modulated onto an intermediate frequency to avoid low-frequency noise and bypass stringent optical phase-locking requirements. However, a rigorous analysis of the quantum security implications of the digital down-conversion algorithm remains absent. In this paper, we investigate the algorithm process from the perspective of quantum operator evolution, revealing that the frequency folding effect inherent in down-conversion inevitably mixes the image-frequency information into the baseband signal. To address this issue, we propose a novel operator reconstruction detection scheme based on dual-path digital heterodyne receiver. By performing a non-equal weighted combination of the output operators along two optical paths in the digital domain, this scheme perfectly cancels out the image-frequency operator physically. The robust receiver architecture preserves the baseband noise-suppression advantages, inherently achieves perfect mode balancing for asymmetric optical detection losses, and fundamentally closes the image-frequency crosstalk. Practical experiments have validated the feasibility of the proposed architecture and its effective suppression of image-frequency noise, achieving a performance of 11.4 Mbps @ 42 km. This work lays a solid theoretical and algorithmic foundation for future high-performance, highly secure digital continuous-variable quantum key distribution systems.

title: Volume Rendering with Metric--Phase Fields for Thin Structures and Sign-Ambiguous Geometry
abstract: Neural implicit surface methods that couple volume rendering with signed distance functions (SDFs), such as VolSDF and NeuS, achieve high-quality multi-view reconstruction for watertight objects. However, these approaches rely on a globally consistent inside-outside partition of space. This assumption becomes fragile for thin structures (e.g., sheets, tubes, and thin walls) and can break down for sign-ambiguous geometry (e.g., surfaces with boundary, non-manifold junctions, and closely spaced surface components), often resulting in spurious closures or loss of fine structures. Unsigned distance field (UDF) formulations relax the global sign requirement and better support non-watertight geometry, but are substantially harder to optimize. We propose PhaseSurf, a neural volume rendering framework built on Metric-Phase Fields (MPFs). MPFs decompose geometry into a nonnegative metric field capturing unsigned proximity and a continuous phase field providing a soft sign cue. By coupling the two through residual phase injection, MPFs yield a signed composite implicit function with stable near-surface gradients while retaining UDF-like robustness in sign-ambiguous regions. evidence.title: Volume Rendering with Metric--Phase Fields for Thin Structures and Sign-Ambiguous Geometry
evidence.abstract: Neural implicit surface methods that couple volume rendering with signed distance functions (SDFs), such as VolSDF and NeuS, achieve high-quality multi-view reconstruction for watertight objects. However, these approaches rely on a globally consistent inside-outside partition of space. This assumption becomes fragile for thin structures (e.g., sheets, tubes, and thin walls) and can break down for sign-ambiguous geometry (e.g., surfaces with boundary, non-manifold junctions, and closely spaced surface components), often resulting in spurious closures or loss of fine structures. Unsigned distance field (UDF) formulations relax the global sign requirement and better support non-watertight geometry, but are substantially harder to optimize. We propose PhaseSurf, a neural volume rendering framework built on Metric-Phase Fields (MPFs). MPFs decompose geometry into a nonnegative metric field capturing unsigned proximity and a continuous phase field providing a soft sign cue. By coupling the two through residual phase injection, MPFs yield a signed composite implicit function with stable near-surface gradients while retaining UDF-like robustness in sign-ambiguous regions. This design enables direct iso-surface extraction using standard Marching Cubes and avoids the failure modes of both pure SDF- and UDF-based formulations. We further introduce MPF-specific training losses that enforce metric consistency, stabilize phase transitions near the interface, and suppress spurious geometry in free space. Experiments on multi-view datasets with thin structures and sign-ambiguous geometry show that PhaseSurf produces more stable reconstructions and higher-quality geometry than UDF-based methods and recent 3DGS pipelines, while avoiding artifacts typical of SDF-based approaches.

title: EXPERIMENTAL COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF NAIVE BAYES AND RULE BASED DECISION TREE PERFORMANCE IN ATTRIBUTIVE CLASSIFICATION OF SCHOLARLY ARTICLES
abstract: Document classification categorizes documents based on their attributes or contents to determine how they will be stored, retrieved, and shared. Improper classification of documents can lead to significant waste of time, resources, productivity, and efficiency in organizational information management systems. This study presents the Experimental Comparative Analysis (ECA) of Naive Bayes Model (NBM) and Rule-Based Decision Tree Model (RBDTM) in the classification of journal articles based on their attributes such as Name of Journal (NOJ) regarded as the specific domain, Peer Reviewed (PR) status, Volume Information (VI), the Title (T), Author Names (AN), Digital Object Identifier (DOI) and Keywords (KW). The models were trained based on direct algebraic solutions, saved parameters, and deterministic passes without gradient descent updates, using supervised Machine Learning (ML) approach and K-fold validation sampling technique for training and testing. Performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1-score, program execution time, information retrieval response time, memory usage, and confusion matrix were used for analysis and evaluation. The training and testing datasets were obtained from open-licensed, peer-reviewed journal articles from Africa, Asia, the United States of America, Eastern and Western Europe. The average test results at the baseline threshold showed that the NBM performed better than the RBDTM in accuracy, recall, and F1-score (68%, 68%, and 80.6%, respectively); both models achieved 100% precision and 0% specificity. In contrast, RBDTM outperformed NBM in program execution time, information retrieval response time, and memory usage (17.19ms, 7.44ms, and 0.13%, respectively). At the optimized threshold, both models tied with 100% accuracy, 100% precision, 100% recall, 0% specificity, and 100% F1-score, but the RBDTM demonstrated the best overall performance with 18.2ms program execution time, 7.74ms information retrieval response time, and 0.14% memory usage.

title: Code and data for "Physically constrained adversarial attacks on neural-network classifiers of quantum phases: symmetry-breaking versus topological order"
abstract: Simulation code, generated datasets, trained network weights, raw results files and figure scripts accompanying the manuscript “Physically constrained adversarial attacks on neural-network classifiers of quantum phases: symmetry-breaking versus topological order”, submitted to Quantum Frontiers. Contents: Monte Carlo generation of two-dimensional Ising configurations (L = 16); generation of Su–Schrieffer–Heeger chains (N = 96) with chiral-symmetric hopping disorder and real-space winding number; MLP, periodic CNN and Z2-symmetrised CNN classifiers; FGSM/PGD, greedy spin-flip and Hamiltonian-level hopping-disorder attacks; adversarial training; and all results from which the figures and tables in the paper are produced. See README.md for the file list and reproduction steps. Tested with Python 3.13, NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, PyTorch 2.14 (CPU) and Matplotlib 3.11.

title: QuantumShield AI: An AI-Powered Post-Quantum Cryptography Recommendation Platform
abstract: The finalization of the NIST post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), with FN-DSA (draft FIPS 206), has shifted the migration question from whether to adopt PQC to which standard best fits an organization's operational and regulatory context. Existing studies benchmark these algorithms thoroughly but stop short of a selection mechanism, leaving practitioners to interpret timing tables by hand. This paper presents QuantumShield AI, a decision-support platform that formalizes PQC algorithm selection as a multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) problem, encodes the selection task as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO), and solves it with the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) on a statevector simulator, cross-validated by an exact classical solver. Six industry profiles — banking, healthcare, IoT/edge, government, e-commerce, and defense supply criteria weightings grounded in sector requirements. The framework is delivered as a three-tier platform combining a React front end, a Spring Boot service layer with JWT-based role-controlled access, and a Python/Qiskit quantum microservice over PostgreSQL. To our knowledge this is the first framework to operationalize selection across the complete finalized NIST portfolio, converting sector requirements into an auditable, reproducible recommendation. Across all six profiles the QAOA solution recovers the exact optimum (approximation ratio = 1.0), validating the pipeline; we are explicit that at the four-algorithm scale this certifies correctness rather than quantum advantage, and the QUBO–QAOA formulation is carried as a forward-compatible path to NP-hard enterprise-portfolio selection. The contribution is a novel, deployable decision methodology and its engineered realization.
